question.leadin: This woman was the last ruler of the Ptolemaic [tall-uh-may-ik] dynasty.
question.text: Name this last queen of independent Egypt before it was conquered by the Romans.
question.clue: Drinking pearls dissolved in vinegar apocryphally won a bet for this ruler, whose short-lived successor was Caesarion.

swap.text: This river has its origins in the Blue and White rivers and, thanks to the Aswan Dam, is not flooding as much as it used to.
swap.clue: The Bari and related peoples migrated up this river after the end of the baqt ("bukt") treaty, which caused kingdoms led from Soba and Dongola to decline and allowed the Funj Sultanate to expand along this river.

question.text: The discovery of this pharaoh's tomb was monumental because it was nearly fully intact, with very few artifacts stolen by grave robbers. Howard Carter discovered the tomb of this pharaoh, the youngest ruler of Egypt.
question.clue: This pharaoh moved Egypt's capital back to Thebes from Amarna and reinstated the worship of traditional Egyptian gods.

swap.text: This young pharaoh, the son of Akhenaten, had his tomb excavated by Howard Carter.
swap.clue: George Herbert financed a mission in the Valley of the Kings that stumbled upon the resting place of this Pharaoh, son of Akhenaten.

question.leadin: Alan Gardiner hypothesized that this symbol derived from the image of a sandal, with the top loop being the strap around the ankle.
question.text: Give the original-language term for this ancient Egyptian symbol, which resembles a T with a loop on top of it. It represents life.
question.clue: The phrase crux ansata is sometimes used synonymously with this word.

swap.text: In addition to the Spartans, belligerents from Thespiae and this city were present at the last stand. This city's Sacred Band was an elite military unit composed of gay lovers.
swap.clue: Troops from this city employed the "cutting off the snake's head" technique to defeat Cleombrotus of Sparta.

question.text: Prior to the Great Pyramid's construction, this Third Dynasty ruler was buried at Saqqara in a step pyramid designed by his deified chancellor Imhotep.
question.clue: An official of this pharaoh communes with the god Khnum to stop a seven-year flood, as recorded on the Famine Stela.

swap.leadin: Much like Chip Beall, the people of this time period were anti-pyramidal, eschewing ostentatious tombs for ones cut out of rock, which were easier to conceal and protect.
swap.text: Name this unsteady time in Egyptian history beginning with unification under Mentuhotep I and ending with Egypt being conquered by the Hyksos; that is, the first and second Intermediate Periods.
swap.clue: The fnal rulers of this period were called the Xois Dynasty since they moved the capital there.

question.leadin: This son of Amenhotep III and pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty started a religious controversy by promoting monotheistic worship of a disk-shaped sun god.
question.text: Name this man who also moved the capital to Amarna.
question.clue: This man wrote a "Great Hymn" to his namesake and was possibly succeeded by Smenkhkare.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about legendary snakes in African history.
swap.text: This Egyptian ruler legendarily committed suicide by having a snake bite her to avoid participating in a triumph for Octavian.
swap.clue: Rome transitioned from a republic to an empire following Augustus Caesar's defeat of this non-Roman ruler at the Battle of Actium.

question.text: This Egyptian historian may have conflated Tut with king Rathotis. He wrote the Aegyptiaca during the Ptolemaic era and among other claims, suggested the pharaoh Menes was killed by a hippopotamus.
question.clue: Continuations of this priest's historical work have been written by the Libyan Apion and Chaeremon.

swap.leadin: The last inscription in this writing system is the Graffito of Esmet-Akhom in the late 4th Century CE.
swap.text: Name this script. Jean-Francois Champollion used the Rosetta Stone to decipher this form of writing, which was included on the stone along with Greek and Demotic.

question.text: This group is often credited with introducing chariot warfare to ancient Egypt. This group ruled over the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt from the city of Avaris.
question.clue: In a satirical story, a ruler of these people complains that he can't sleep because of noisy hippos in a letter addressed to Seqenenre ("sek-en-EN-ray") Tao.

swap.text: A Pharaoh's personal name was inscribed inside this symbol, an elongated form of the shen ring motif. This symbol consists of an oval tangent to a straight line.

question.leadin: This figure is depicted on one object preparing to club a figure known as Wash and identified by rebus symbols of a catfish and a chisel.
question.text: Name this ruler depicted on both a namesake macehead and an object used to grind cosmetics, an image that some scholars believe represents the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.
question.clue: The existence of this pharaoh is attested to by a namesake palette that depicts him with two crowns. This pharaoh was the unifier of Upper and Lower Egypt.

swap.text: Historians often lament the incompleteness of Egyptian king lists, such as the one located in this ancient city's Temple of Seti I. Multiple early dynastic pharaohs were interred in this city's Umm El Qa'ab necropolis.
swap.clue: Nekhen rivaled this city, whose Tomb U-j ("U-J") may house the Predynastic Naqada III ruler King Scorpion I near its tombs of the First Dynasty's Thinite kings.

question.leadin: Although his name does not appear on the Turin King List, most scholars dispute Manetho's claim that this pharaoh ruled for 66 years.
question.text: Name this Old Kingdom pharaoh. A causeway links the Great Sphinx constructed by this man to his pyramid, which he literally named after his own greatness.
question.clue: This son of Khufu succeeded his half-brother Djedefre and, much like Khufu and Menkaure, he built his own great pyramid at Giza. According to Manetho and Herodotus, he ruled for 66 years and may have also built the Sphinx.

swap.leadin: The uniquely realistic statues of the third pharaoh of this name depict him as an angry old man with oversized ears.
swap.text: Give this name of three Twelfth Dynasty pharaohs. Herodotus gave this name's Greek equivalent to a pharaoh who supposedly erected genitalia-topped columns to mock the cities he conquered in Asia Minor and Thrace.
swap.answerHtml: Senusret [or Sesostris; or Senwosret; accept Senusret I or Senusret II or Senusret III]
swap.clue: The pyramid at el-Lahun, or Kahun, was designed for the second pharaoh of this name, who also built a great dike there. Except for its last female ruler Sobekneferu, the entire Twelfth Dynasty consisted only of pharaohs with this name or Amenemhat.

question.leadin: This woman invented an early double-boiler, now culinarily referred to as this woman's namesake bath.
question.text: Identify this first-century woman, who Zosimos of Panopolis regarded as the first alchemist in the Western world. She is known for a namesake alchemical axiom stating "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth."
question.answerHtml: Mary the Jewess [accept Mary the Prophetess; accept Maria the Copt; accept Maria Hebraea; accept Maria Prophetissa; accept Māriyya al-Qibṭiyya; prompt on Mary alone]

swap.text: Seqenenre's other son Ahmose established the New Kingdom by driving the Hyksos out of this capital city of theirs, which was absorbed into the city of Pi-Ramesses with the advent of the Nineteenth Dynasty.
